speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 3, to provide for pay for statutory holidays for employees and for pay for work performed on statutory holidays.

speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide that all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction shall receive their regular pay for at least eight statutory holidays each year without having to work on those holidays. maintopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to establish a minimum rate of wages with respect to all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. This bill provides that such minimum rate of wages shall be $1 per hour. The bill also provides that its terms do not affect any employees whose rate of wages is higher than the minimum established by this legislation. However, any rate of wages less favourable to employees than $1 per hour is superseded by this bill.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
I should like to address this question to the Minister of Transport. What plans has the minister

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: DISCUSSIONS CONCERNING DEEP SEA FACILITIES AT LAKEHEAD
speechtext:
In the first place I feel sure that the feelings of the Port Arthur city council do not need any assuaging, because when I went to the lakehead some few weeks ago I was received very cordially by the officials of both Port Arthur and Fort William. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED OFFER OF SPEAKERSHIP TO HON. MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Prime Minister. Is it true that the Prime Minister has requested the socialist member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to be the permanent Speaker of this House of Commons? If there has been any correspondence on the subject I would ask that copies of it be tabled.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: REPORTED OFFER OF SPEAKERSHIP TO HON. MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I answer that first
categorically. No; there was no offer to the hon. gentleman to be permanent Speaker. I am one of those who believe that action should be taken, having regard to what took place in the last two or three sessions, to bring about a degree of authority in the Speaker that would be above partisan consideration. During the election campaign and prior thereto I pointed out that one of the matters that deserved consideration was the appointment of a permanent Speaker and, if possible, when that unanimity of opinion -could be secured in the House of Commons, to bring about permanence in the speakership. However, that has not been achieved, in order to place the speakership above the importunities of anyone in this house, and in order that the Speaker would never in the future, during this parliament, be in any way considered to be, or placed in, the unenviable position in which those who now sit opposite to us placed the former Speaker.
The hon. gentleman mentioned the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. There was no offer of a permanent speakership in any way inherent in the offer. What I said was this, and I will table the correspondence if my hon. friend is willing and if he expresses his willingness now. I asked the hon. member whether, because of the fact that he was regarded as an authority on parliamentary rules, he would allow me to place his name in nomination; and if he were chosen by the House of Commons, would he accept the appointment. That is the total and summary answer to my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I do want to make clear one thing that may not have been clear in my earlier remarks. I am very anxious to table these two letters. It has been agreed by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that they should be tabled, and with your permission it can be done at once.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, October 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. A. R. Smith (Calgary South) for an address to Her Majesty the Queen in reply to her speech at the opening of the session.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make my first comments on the address on behalf of the official opposition in this house, I should like to repeat my earlier statement that we deeply appreciate the historic circumstance that for the first time in the history of the Canadian parliament the speech from the throne was delivered by the sovereign in person. We welcomed the Queen in this parliament because among other reasons to be valid every act of this parliament must have the Queen's assent, and the royal assent is not an empty formality. It is true that the sovereign, under our British parliamentary system, acts only on the advice of ministers who are responsible to the elected branch of our parliament, but the crown is nonetheless an essential and a vital part of parliament itself.
The crown is a symbol of the constitutional evolution of our parliamentary tradition and also of our unity as a nation. The
9669S-4
The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent presence of Her Majesty the Queen in our parliament here in Ottawa has for us given new life to that symbol.
I have already referred to the fact that I appear in this house in a new capacity. I must confess that I was disappointed by the results of the recent election. I do not propose, however, to dwell on that disappointment nor do I intend to speculate upon the reasons for those results. The results speak for themselves. The party which I have had the honour to lead for the past nine years accepted those results loyally, without hesitation, in what we believe is the true spirit of our parliamentary system.
I do feel that all Canadians have a right to be proud of the ease and smoothness with which the change of government was accomplished as soon as possible after the full results of the general election were known. As we look around us in the world today we note that there are not too many countries where a government which has been entrenched in office for over 20 years could be changed so speedily and with so little confusion. The fact that this change took place in the manner it did may perhaps give many of our fellow citizens a deeper faith in the strength of our parliamentary tradition and our parliamentary institutions and the devotion that all of us feel to that tradition and to those institutions.
I should like to do in parliament what I have done out of parliament and congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) upon the vigour of his campaign and upon the support he was able to enlist for himself and for his party in the recent election. The Prime Minister does not expect me to wish him any long tenure of his present office, but I do say sincerely that I appreciate the way the Prime Minister has preserved not merely the letter but the spirit of the amenities of our parliamentary system. In all of those difficult and delicate arrangements which are inseparable from a change of government the Prime Minister has shown courtesy and consideration which I have appreciated and which I trust will always characterize the relations between party leaders in this parliament.
Perhaps I may be permitted to say that what happened on June 21 was an effective answer to some of the exaggeration about the dangers to parliament which we heard so much about before June 10.
The speech from the throne forecasts steps by the government to make both houses of parliament more effective in the discharge of their responsibilities to the people of Canada. All hon. members have an equal interest in having parliament function as

The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent an effective instrument in the services of the Canadian people and we on this side of the house hope that the government's plans for making parliament more effective were not being foreshadowed by the Prime Minister in recent speeches he made in Charlottetown and Montreal of which the newspaper reports give the impression he was suggesting that the house should accept virtually without question whatever program the government laid before it.
No; that is a misinterpretation.

I hope
that is not an accurate forecast of what the government had in mind.
Hon. members are aware of the decision I had with great regret to announce on September 6 that I did not feel I had the strength and vigour necessary to lead my party in another general election and for that reason I felt the right course was to relinquish the leadership of my party as soon as a successor could be chosen in the appropriate manner. I doubt whether any party leader in the history of our country has enjoyed greater loyalty or more widespread support throughout the whole of his leadership than it has been my lot to enjoy since I became leader of the Liberal party in August, 1948. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, it was not easy to reach the conclusion that so soon after the party had suffered its first reverse I would have to give up the responsibility and the honour of leadership. I reached the conclusion, however, that if, as I was advised, the state of my health was such that I could not reasonably expect to lead the party effectively in another general election campaign, it was important for the effectiveness of the role of the Liberal party in our parliamentary system and therefore in the interest of the country that the leadership should be assumed by someone with the necessary strength and vigour to fully discharge that task. Once I had reached that decision, and of course I alone could make it, I felt the right thing to do was to communicate it to the public without delay, so that is what I decided had to be done.
I mention these circumstances, because they do have a bearing on parliament. In this house I occupy the office of Leader of the Opposition and I hope to continue to occupy that office until a new permanent leader of our party has been selected. Once that selection has been made I shall, of course, immediately relinquish the office of Leader of the Opposition to my successor. In the meanwhile I shall endeavour to discharge the constitutional duties of that office to the best
of my abilities, fortified by the knowledge that I speak in this house for a united party which, as recently as June 10, still commanded substantially more popular support than any other political party in the country.
In assuming my new task as Leader of the Opposition I am comforted by the fact that, in spite of what has been said in answer to questions yesterday and today in the house, and in spite of the fact members of the present government and their supporters campaigned on the slogan that it was time for a change, they did seem singularly reluctant to make important changes in the policies or methods we followed when we sat on the other side. One member of the government after another has asserted he found little to change in the policies or administration of his department.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) paid tribute to the efficiency of our defence forces and, as recently as October 6th, indicated that there would be no fundamental changes in our forces. However, rumours appearing recently in the press seem to have caused some uncertainty in the public mind on this score. The Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Fulton) has apparently sought to give the impression he was following our practices. Two of the harshest critics of our administration, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) seem to have gone out of their way to praise the departments over which they preside. Even the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) seems to have found merits in the trans-Canada highway in its present state that were not too apparent to many of us on this side of the house. Indeed, the one minister who seems to have found serious fault with the previous administration, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), claims to have discovered many examples of waste and extravagance in the administration of the various departments. We shall all await with interest the particular examples the Minister of Finance is able to disclose.
We on this side of the house will rejoice with him if he is able to bring about any substantial economies without impairing essential services. Both Mr. Harris and Mr. Abbott before him were always trying to do this, and they succeeded in keeping the growth of expenditures well below the growth of the country during the past ten years. It is, I agree with the present incumbent of that important portfolio, the duty of any minister of finance to keep down expenditures as much as that can be done without impairing the services that the public needs and wants.

Perhaps the most heartening of all these assertions was the apparent endorsement given to the external policies of the Liberal government by the new Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) on the day he was sworn into office. Until about a year ago the discussion of external affairs in this house was generally carried on in a non-partisan spirit and I, for one, was very glad that the minister should have stated so definitely that he approved of the policies that were followed a year ago. We all hope Doctor Smith will continue to exhibit the admirably objective and non-partisan attitude which he proclaimed on the day he became a member of the government.
In view of the statements made before June 10, we have heard with surprise from the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) speeches about the wheat problem which, when compared with previous speeches, have echoed the very words used about this problem by his distinguished predecessor. Indeed, in so far as wheat is concerned, the only thing that seems to have changed since June 10 is that we appear to be selling less and less wheat than we were previously.
There has been from the Prime Minister the much-heralded pronouncement in the United States on Canadian-United States relations. Those of us who have compared his pronouncements at Dartmouth college with the speeches made in the United States not long before June 10 by the former minister of trade and commerce, and even since June 10 by the former secretary of state for external affairs, could only rub our eyes and wonder whether anything was changed because there seemed to be nothing whatever in the Prime Minister's speech that had not already been said, and said very well and at least as forcefully, by members of the Liberal government.
The other day the four ministers returned from a meeting in Washington and brought back a promise from the United States government not to resume the form of wheat disposal by barter which the United States had already abandoned while we were still in office. This seemed to be really all that was accomplished, unless there was something achieved that was not mentioned in the communique. One might wonder if those who voted for a change on June 10 really wanted anything more than a change of faces, because so far that seems to be the most that has been obtained, except perhaps a growing feeling of uneasiness about the future. You would not expect me to admit that that was a very substantial change for the better.
96698-4i
The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent
I should not neglect any longer to compliment the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of the address, and to compliment them sincerely upon the admirable style and delivery of their maiden efforts in the house. The house, of course, always listens with sympathy to a newly-elected member making his first effort to catch its ear, and both hon. members acquitted themselves in a manner which promises well for their future contributions to our debates. It is not customary for the Leader of the Opposition to praise the contents of the speeches of the mover and seconder of the address and on this occasion particularly as I, too, am a novice, I shall not depart from precedent. I cannot, of course, share their understandable admiration for the new government which they feel they were elected to support.
I believe I have reached a point where I should indicate, as precisely as I can, what the attitude of the Liberal opposition will be to the new government during the present session when I expect to be responsible for leading the opposition. It is over 22 years since the Liberal party was last in opposition. In the 22 years Canada has enjoyed-I use a word that I believe will become more widely used in that connection as time passes-I say in the 22 years that Canada has enjoyed a Liberal government we as Liberals have prided ourselves on the fact that every item of the program placed before the public in each successive campaign has been implemented in full whenever it was possible for the government or for the parliament of Canada acting alone to implement it. The only items in our Liberal programs which have not been fully implemented are those which have required provincial co-operation, which was not always forthcoming, or the co-operation of the governments of other countries or of international bodies. Everything we have undertaken to do that could be done by a government here in Ottawa acting on its own has been accomplished.
This is a record of which we are justly proud. We are also proud of the fact that in these past twenty years the people of Canada have come to take it for granted that the government of Canada acts in good faith and carries out its undertakings to the people. I believe that the good faith in fulfilling undertakings that the public has received from the Liberal government they will now expect to receive from a Conservative government. I understand that is also the view of the present Prime Minister.
Of course it may be argued that the situation is somewhat different because the present government has not a majority of its
44	HOUSE OF
The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent own supporters in this house. That is true. The Conservative party was a long way from receiving a majority either of the popular vote or of the seats in parliament on June 10 last. But as far as its promises to the people are concerned, that should not be a substantial handicap to the government. Almost all of the Conservative promises were echoed by the two smaller parties represented in this house. Indeed, the most substantial difference between the Conservative party and the smaller parties in that regard is that the smaller parties were making even larger promises.
Since June 10 I understand that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and other members of his party have pledged their support to the government in fulfilling the promises, at least to the extent to which they themselves made them. To many Liberals some of the promises have seemed to be somewhat imprudent and some of them seem to be even impractical; but the fundamental position of the Liberal party is and always has been that the people by their votes have the right to control their own government.
We do not think that a Liberal minority in parliament has any more right to frustrate the will of the people by an obstructive attitude than has a Conservative minority or a C.C.F. minority. We believe that an opposition should state its position vigorously and honestly and that it should do its utmost to persuade a majority that when it objects to legislation, its objections are sound. But in the final analysis our view is that the will of the majority in parliament and, even more, of the majority in the country, should prevail. Indeed, our view is that a minority in parliament should not seek to obstruct the will of the majority unless the minority believes-and that may be possible at times- that there is at stake a principle of such importance to the nation that the minority should do everything in its power to bring the question before the electorate itself for a decision.
In the case of the Prime Minister's election promises we feel that the Liberal opposition should not attempt to substitute itself for the will of the majority expressed so recently in the general election. It is a fundamental Liberal belief that the people are entitled to have promises made to them by a successful political party implemented, and implemented in full.
I do not intend to detain the house with a catalogue of the promises made by the Prime Minister in the recent campaign. The speech from the throne forecasts legislation to implement several of these promises. I do not refer to the sections of the speech


which deal with international and commonwealth affairs. Apart from the reference to the Mont Tremblant conference, to which I shall refer later, the rest of these sections of the speech could just as well have been put there by a Liberal government. Indeed, many of the phrases are mere echoes of earlier speeches; and I am not suggesting that they are any the worse for that.
As for the measures forecast to increase old age security and other social benefits, naturally every true Liberal will welcome them in principle. Our sole concern will be to see how they fit into the whole financial picture and how far the government will take effective measures to control the rise in the cost of living which, if unchecked, could easily take away all the advantages of the proposed increases.
I think my right hon. friend would agree that the vague language used about benefits for farmers and fishermen is perhaps better suited to a party manifesto than to a legislative program, but when it is translated into a legislative program we shall see just what it can mean and what its effect can be. Like the farmers and the fishermen themselves, the opposition will be eager to see what, if anything, the proposed legislation really adds up to.
As for cash advances for farm stored wheat, it is our view that the farmers of the prairies and the country would be much more interested in the progress being made in selling the wheat.
There is nothing new in the so-called national development program as outlined in the speech from the throne except the undertaking to assist in financing Beechwood and the forecast of early discussions about beginning the South Saskatchewan dam.
Evidently part of the burden of the wider program for producing and transmitting power in the Atlantic provinces which we felt should be financed entirely out of the federal treasury is being pushed back on the provinces. In the speech from the throne there was just the gentlest hint of tax changes. The language of the speech was in singular contrast to the vigorous and forthright language used by the Minister of Finance in June.
Let me recall his statement as reported by the Canadian Press in the Montreal Gazette of June 26. The article is entitled "Tax Reductions, Pensions Boosts in Fall Budget" and reads as follows:
Ottawa, June 25-(CP) Finance Minister Donald Fleming said tonight he plans to bring down a new budget next fall to reduce taxes, increase old age pension and possibly curb government spending.
The new Progressive Conservative fiscal chief said also in an interview that he will be moving

toward easing of the federal "tight-money" policy as quickly as possible with the hope of reviving Canada's housing slump.
"There very definitely must be an early relaxation of the rigors of the tight-money policy," said the 52-year old Toronto lawyer on whose shoulders have fallen the job of developing a financial policy to fulfil Prime Minister Diefenbaker's election promises.
The same report goes on to state that the Minister of Finance recalled that during the election campaign the Prime Minister had promised to reduce taxes, increase old age pensions and bring about a fair distribution for provinces and municipalities of revenue from joint federal-provincial tax fields. Then there is this direct quotation:
"These promises will be fulfilled," Mr. Fleming said, observing that in. each case the promises required action of the finance department.
We are all looking forward to the presentation of this budget and to a full debate on the case the Minister of Finance will present at that time.
From time to time I have noticed from press rumours that the government intends to make important changes in the fiscal policy of this country without giving the elected representatives of the Canadian people an opportunity for a full debate which, under our parliamentary system, is afforded by the presentation of a budget. I refuse to believe that a government whose leading members made so much of their attachment to the rights of parliament would seriously propose, both to alter the tax structure of the country and to increase expenditures substantially without giving parliament every opportunity afforded by the rules to consider the whole financial picture and to debate fully the benefits of proposed changes upon the economy.
In the budget proposals we will await with particular interest the proposal for implementing the promises which the Prime Minister made, all across the country, to arrange for a substantial increase in the revenues of the provinces. That is a matter which we have studied very carefully, over the years. We may not have been able to reach the best possible conclusion, but we put forth our best efforts. We have therefore been somewhat surprised that the federal-provincial conference which the Prime Minister promised to call immediately after the election should have been delayed now for nearly five months.
We perhaps are entitled to expect also, in accordance with their oft-proclaimed policy of keeping parliament fully informed, that we in parliament would be advised in advance of the proposals that the government will place before the federal-provincial conference. For our part we are proud that it was a Liberal government which established
The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent the principle of equalization payments out of taxes paid by all the Canadian people with the object of placing all the provincial governments in a more nearly equal position to discharge their constitutional obligations. It seems to us that any departure from the principle of equalization will be viewed with alarm in all parts of Canada.
Now may I turn for a moment to the question of trade about which the Prime Minister made a very far-reaching proposal. I refer, of course, to the policy he announced on his return from the meeting of the commonwealth prime ministers in London, namely, that the government will seek to divert 15 per cent of our purchases from the United States to commonwealth countries. I should like to believe that the Prime Minister would not announce such a policy unless he had a concrete plan designed to carry it out. It is true that a few suggestions for increasing United Kingdom sales in Canada were contained in the joint announcement made by the United Kingdom and Canadian ministers on October 4, but I submit, with great respect, that these suggestions do not appear to be very impressive.
For most of the period since the war our government has sought systematically to direct our purchases to the United Kingdom, if they were purchases of things that could not be made at home, and there is nothing new in the suggestion that that policy be pursued. The increasing United Kingdom exports which would result from increasing the $100 exemption for tourists certainly would not go very far, and the high level trade delegation is not something new. For years a committee headed by Mr. James Duncan, and other special missions, have been contributing in the same way to the same end. I am sure that all of us who know Mr. Duncan-and many of us do know him-would believe that he had put forth very serious efforts to make a success of the mission upon which he was engaged and which he headed. It does not seem that any of these things are likely to bring about a diversion of even a small fraction of one per cent of our purchases, much less 15 per cent. We will be very interested to know what is the government's plan for this huge diversion of trade.
It seems to us that there are only three possible ways to bring about a diversion of trade on this scale, if indeed a diversion on this scale is possible at all. The first would be discriminatory increases in tariffs against the United States. Some suggestions have been made that this might be called the Bennett way. I do not think that that is the plan and I think it would create serious difficulties if it were considered as a way to bring about this

The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent desirable result of making it possible for the United Kingdom economy to earn Canadian dollars.
The second way would be by state trading and state control of exports and imports which might be called the soviet way. That certainly is not being contemplated by this government, nor would it be contemplated by any Canadian government as a proper manner in which to handle our trade policies.
The third way is by the reduction or removal of trade barriers between Canada and commonwealth countries, which I suppose you might call the Thorneycroft way. We have been given the impression that the government is not too enthusiastic about that; the Minister of Finance was supposed to have a secret agenda of his own at Mont Tremblant, but so far the Canadian public have not been given any hint of what that agenda might contain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did not have any secret agenda of his own.

Well there was a report published of a press conference with the Minister of Finance, held before the Mont Tremblant meeting, which was progressing splendidly until the newspaper men commenced to ask questions about an agenda and were told that the agenda was on the secret list and that the ways and means were matters that could not be divulged at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was not my agenda.

I would
imagine that the hon. gentleman would not be writing the agenda himself but would be using the assistance of the very competent staff of the Department of Finance and the Department of Trade and Commerce in preparing an agenda for that kind of meeting.
Now the speech from the throne refers to the comradely spirit at Mont Tremblant. Well, this comradely spirit seems to have escaped the notice of press correspondents. Perhaps I might be allowed to cite a comment in the last issue of the Financial Post on October 12 entitled "Months of Grace for Tories Over":
The unfortunate fact is that the Mont Tremblant conference between Canadian and British officials was a great flop.
The whole story of what went on behind the scenes is now available (see page 3 this issue).
The British had prepared very thoroughly for the meeting. The Canadians had not.
The crux of the problem of increasing trade between Canada and Commonwealth countries is in how governments can foster this without running foul of their commitments under GATT.
The British came with their proposal which they had told the Canadians about several weeks before. Their plans got the much over-simplified name of free trade area. Stated baldly that way, it stunned the Canadians, and before it ever got adequately explained, it got buried. Fully explained, it isn't nearly such a startling scheme as it sounds.

This is regrettable because a thorough, unexcited examination might have led somewhere. At least, a sober discussion of it would have laid useful groundwork for future conferences. But the fact is that the cause of commonwealth trade has actually been set back rather than advanced.
What caused the Mont Tremblant fiasco?
Despite the advance warning that the British would announce this proposal, it appears that the Canadians went to the conference without doing nearly enough homework. The big research and analysis machinery available to the government wasn't adequately exploited.
Ottawa observers of the affair are also convinced that the new Canadian cabinet hasn't yet got its working methods organized, that cabinet members are inadequately informed on the Prime Minister's views and on each other's.
One Briton said: "Before the meeting Canadians talked a lot about commonwealth trade, but at the conference they apparently were not prepared to face up to doing anything important about it."
Coming into office after so long a pilgrimage in the wilderness of opposition, the new government was bound to take some time to learn how to run public business smoothly.
But parliament meets next week. The months of grace are over. The new government should take pains to demonstrate to voters that it knows where it is going, that it doesn't make large promises it doesn't know how to fulfil.
I submit that it is time parliament and the Canadian people were told in precise language just what the plans of the government are to divert our trade to commonwealth countries and precisely what is involved in the proposals of the United Kingdom government.
We were told before the election that this trade problem was urgent: surely it cannot be shelved until a commonwealth conference is held some time next year to consider an agenda which is still being kept secret from the people of Canada. On this question of the diversion of trade we in the opposition will not attempt to comment, and no one can comment intelligently until we know what the government really proposes.
We believe the proper function of an opposition which hopes and expects to be in office again is to be fair and frank with the public, to criticize the government vigorously, and to advance alternatives to the policies followed by the government, but not to seek to usurp the functions of the government or to take responsibility for them.
Having the reasonable assurance that the fulfilment of its promises will not be obstructed at the present session of parliament, at least by the official opposition, the government will have no excuse for any failure to carry out that program.
In the special circumstances in which this house finds itself where no party has a majority but where there does seem to be a disposition to give the government the opportunity to bring its legislation before

the house, it does not seem to us in the official opposition to be appropriate to move the traditional vote of want of confidence.
Such a motion could, it seems to me, have only one or other of two effects. If the motion were carried it would deny the government the possibility of attempting to fulfil their promises. If the motion were not carried it would serve merely to put forward some alternative proposition, and the beginning of this session does not seem to be the time for that.
Having decided not to move an amendment ourselves, we do not feel at this time that we should support any amendment to the address moved in any other quarter of the house.
We feel that the government has enunciated a program in the speech from the throne in general terms. No doubt the government has legislation in which we will find more precise, more concrete suggestions than those contained in the speech from the throne, and we think that the government should have the opportunity of producing that legislation. If that legislation is, as it would appear to be, in line with the pre-election promises made by the government which resulted in the situation which induced us to tender our resignation to His Excellency the Governor General then the government should have the opportunity of producing that legislation and making clear to the Canadian public that it is, and always was, its intention to carry out those promises, and that it feels this can be done without any serious effect on the future economy of the Canadian nation.
I am sure the government will have in mind, in all the measures it will be recommending to parliament, the necessity in the interest of the Canadian individual and the Canadian nation of effectively controlling inflation so that increases in expenditure may not become useless because of increases in prices which these expenses were meant to cover.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is naturally with some diffidence that I rise at this time. The Prime Minister said-
Oh, oh.

The Leader of the Opposition-I say immediately that so long was he in the former office that all of us wondered who would be the first to make the slip. I did.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) said he was not going to prophesy a long period of office for us. I remember a prophecy in January of 1957
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker when I occupied for the first time the position which he is occupying now. He then made the prophecy that I would be in that position for a long time. I am glad he did not make any prophecy today, for, after all, on that occasion and since the prophecy did not come true.
But I am not here for the purpose of going over the election. I dislike referring to that, and I would not have done so had the Leader of the Opposition not referred to it, because it is contrary to my inclinations to bring up matters that cause feelings that I do not want hon. members opposite to feel.
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be words of congratulation to yourself on the elevation to the position you now occupy. I say to you my hope is, and it is a sure one, that in the days ahead you will maintain those great traditions of the position which you occupy.
In the last few days we in this parliament have had an experience, to which reference was made by the Leader of the Opposition, of having a visit from Her Majesty the Queen. As she left us today she sent to us and to all of Canada a message warmhearted and appreciative coupled with the hope that it will not be long before she will again be visiting her country as Queen of Canada. I think I can do no better, with the leave of the house, than to table that message, as well as the message which I sent on your behalf and on behalf of the people of Canada to her on her departure.

to indicate some of the general principles that actuated us in proceeding so soon after the election to carry into effect those promises which we made.
We have great responsibilities as a new parliament meeting under circumstances which we inherited as a government. I refer to the trade situation with the United States wherein today we find ourselves, or did in June last, in the position of having an adverse trade balance of $1,300 million, and increasing year by year. We found ourselves in the position where inflation, to which reference was made by the Leader of the Opposition, was increasing. The cost of living had not been met. We found ourselves in the position that various segments of our population, because of the so-called tight-money policy being improperly applied, were hard hit. This policy brought about in various industries in our country a diminution in production and in productivity and a major reduction in employment. These are some of the things that we found we had inherited. We tried to meet the general situation that existed in unemployment and in particular in the housing industry by action to which reference was made this afternoon, by which $150 million was made available for the construction of small houses.
My right hon. friend mentioned the serious situation with regard to the marketing of wheat, the loss of markets. I ask, what did my hon. friends opposite do in the last two or three years while the markets for wheat were being lost? They ridiculed the endeavour on our part to bring about the establishment of sound economic conditions within our country. Throughout the years we asked them whether or not they would take action in connection with the convening of a commonwealth trade and economic conference. I am not going into the details, but from 1950 on they followed the course year by year of shutting their eyes to the situation that was developing in the loss of our trade and at the same time refusing to take effective action, or indeed any action, to meet the situation which was apparent on every hand. My right hon. friend mentioned the fact that we have already laid the foundations for that conference. He and others on the other side of the house said it could not be done. That conference is being called.

That conference will
achieve many of the aims that we have in mind. Certainly there is no reason whatsoever for the attitude taken by the former government of refusing to do anything, to deny the existence of those things and, having denied them for the past three or four
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker years, now point out to us as the legatees of their failure to act that the things that they did not achieve in years have not been attained in a matter of months.

Did they act? I am not going into the particulars on this occasion. The Minister of Agriculture and others will deal with it. The Canadian farmer found himself in a position where his market in Canada was unfairly challenged by imports into Canada at prices that gave every indication of having been based on other than ordinary commercial grounds, and everywhere across this country the former government failed to act in that regard.

-for several years. The present government when it came into power acted as far as it could within the limitations that must necessarily confine its action until the convening of parliament. I am sure nobody will say that it was improper on our part to postpone the calling of parliament until October 14 in order to permit the events of the last few days to take place; for, after all, the plans had been made long in advance of the election campaign and it would have been, in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of the Leader of the Opposition, most improper to have done anything to change those plans in that regard.
I mention our program in general, what we intend to do, some of the ideas that we have, and I place before parliament in a general outline the development of those policies which we advocated while in opposition. I am going to start with a reference to the social policy. Our legislative program in this regard speaks for itself; it is in keeping with our philosophy, the need of action being taken, the need of action that should have been taken a great deal earlier, and effective action, in order to do something on behalf of those older citizens of our country who because of the very fact raised by the right honourable gentleman, the inflationary trend, found themselves caught in an impossible position.
Yet, what could they do? Knowing the situation they acted, but they acted in such

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker a way that it in no way met the dire position in which many of our elder citizens found themselves. As has been set out in the speech from the throne, we intend to place before parliament measures to improve the lot of the senior members of our society; to increase old age security pensions and to shorten the period of residence required to qualify for them. Changes will be proposed also in the terms of assistance in so far as the Old Age Assistance Act is concerned, the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act. Further changes will be made on behalf of the war veterans in the payment of war veterans' allowances.
These things would have been passed by any previous parliament if it had not been for the fact that the government of my right hon. friend refused to act in this connection and the members who supported him stood behind him in his refusal to act. My right hon. friend spoke of parliament and asked whether changes would be brought about. He spoke of the need for full debate in parliament and I could not be more in agreement with him. There is need for careful examination, full consideration and debate that is not muzzled in anticipation by the application of closure.
I mention that as one of the most serious examples of the curtailment of the ancient rights of parliament. Apparently my right hon. friend looks back upon the course of action followed in 1956 with some regret, for in indicating to us the need for full discussion he pointed out, and properly so, that the essence of parliamentary government is full discussion. You say, what are we going to do about that? Well closure had its place, if properly used, in order to prevent an unjustifiable action on the part of the opposition as against the government of the day after a debate lasting for a very considerable period of time. We found out, however, that closure, necessary as it has been proven to be in times past, not only in our own parliament but in other parliaments within the commonwealth, under our rules constitutes an open invitation to the curtailment of fair and reasonable debate, indeed to the imprisonment of parliament by the government.
During the election campaign I said, and I am unchanged in this viewpoint, that having regard to its potential danger, as was evidenced so clearly so short a time ago, we intend at the first opportunity to move the necessary motion in order to remove closure from the rules of the House of Commons, to the end that parliament will be restored to something of its ancient glory. That is the


first step. We have a tremendous responsibility in this parliament to restore in the hearts of the people something of the prestige of parliament. I am not entering into a discussion as to who was responsible, I am saying that if we are to make this institution the great and abiding institution that it should be to fashion freedom the responsibility will fall on each and every one in this parliament to so conduct himself that, in co-operation, we together, without in any way measuring the responsibility of any member of this house, will make our contribution to the restoration of this parliament to its proper position.
I mentioned the question of social security. I mention now the next matter to which reference is made, the subject of agriculture. I am merely going to give a general idea of some of the steps we shall take in this regard. Naturally I cannot reveal the particulars of the legislative program. I point out, however, that because parliament was not to sit until October 14 one of our first acts in order to meet the situation in which the western farmer found himself, with a vast accumulation of wheat-yes, underestimated by the last government by 75 million bushels which we only ascertained since coming into power-was to continue the loan legislation. This would meet the needs of those who chose to use the available facilities until such time as parliament might meet.
I am hoping that my hon. friends in all parts of the house will agree within the next few days, in view of the serious situation in western Canada, on the need of doing something to advance the legislation even prior to the completion of the present debate. As a matter of fact, I would not have made that suggestion if it had not been indicated there is to be no challenge so far as the official opposition is concerned. Since that is so, there is no reason now why we should not, at the earliest possible date, proceed with the introduction of the resolution and, as soon as possible, bring about the enactment of legislation if parliament will accept the recommendation of this government.
My right hon. friend said that markets were better than cash advances. I agree with him, but where have the markets been? What does one do about the 700 million bushels piled up-not under this government? It was a very great thought to place before parliament the superiority of markets and sales to advances. We supported advances when we were in opposition. We believed they were necessary. We stated that the loan system would not be acceptable. I think, in general, the farm communities of

the western provinces agreed with our contention that the loan system was one that placed the farmer in the position of actually having to pay for a loan on his earnings because he could sell only through the government or its agencies. We intend to introduce this legislation at the earliest possible date.
We intend as well, as has been outlined, through the necessary legislation to lay the foundation for the stabilization of agricultural prices at reasonable levels, taking into consideration market conditions and also the costs of production. We intend to proceed with that program as a safeguard program on behalf of the farmer, as a beginning of a long-term policy to bring about security and stability to the farming population of this country. It is a positive program beginning with the legislation which we will introduce, to be expanded on the basis of experience, which after all is necessary and requisite if the legislation is to be effectual.
In addition to the fact that the farmers have not had stability, one of the major causes of disaffection has been the fact that-this is somewhat different from the situation in the United States where the farmer's share of the consumer dollar has been going up-in Canada in the past seven or eight years the farmer's share of the consumer dollar has been going down. The farmers have been asking for an investigation in this connection for the purpose of arriving at a true conclusion or for an actual explanation of the reason for this peculiar paradoxical course having regard to what is happening in the United States. In order to bring about the beginnings of an investigation of this situation I believe that members of parliament themselves in committee might make an investigation into this matter. If at any time, because of the complexities and difficulties which are incident to the examination, it is found that the matter is too widespread and too complex for a committee to handle, in that case we should certainly consider the setting up of a royal commission to investigate this matter to the end tha* as a result of that investigation and of the recommendations made the action necessary and requisite could be taken.
As far as the agricultural policy is concerned, I mentioned earlier that we had taken emergent action. We took emergent action in July by placing turkeys under price support. We took action by import control some days later in order to prevent Canada's farmers and producers of turkeys from being actually inundated by vast imports that had been increasing over the last several years. In addition to that, in so far
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker as fowl is concerned, we place fowl under price support and also under import control. Both of these actions have received the approval of organized agriculture.
As well action was taken under import control in reference to dry skim milk, the import provisions to continue in effect until May 31, 1958. This was the only action that we could take consistent with the responsibility of parliament and of parliamentary control.
Then there is the next matter to which I wish to make reference and this has to do with the question of a national development policy. I am not going into detail in this connection except to say this. Throughout the last number of years we have been advocating a policy to raise the horizons of the Canadian people, to give Canadians some conception and vision of the greatness of the future, to bring about a policy of co-operation as between the central government and the provincial governments When they ask for co-operation in order to enable the formulation of a national development policy whereby our resources may be developed for the maximum benefit of Canada. In that connection we must move in those areas that are particularly affected and find themselves in a position below the level of the general register of advancement and development in other parts of Canada. As an immediate start upon a program of more extensive development in the Atlantic provinces, you will be asked to authorize, in joint action with the provincial governments, the creation of facilities for the production and transmission of cheaper electric power in those provinces.

New Brunswick friends in the Conservative party have been asking for action in this regard. No action was taken. My right hon. friend mentioned the South Saskatchewan dam. I am sure that if at any time the right hon. gentleman had accepted the advice of the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) there would have been no question as to whether or not that development plan was feasible, indeed more than that was necessary for the diversification of industry within the province of Saskatchewan and to provide in addition thereto the restoration of large land areas which for many years have had successive periods of drought and of plenty.


Various plans have been offered as far as this government is concerned as a result of the examination made by the engineers and on the basis of reports the feasibility of this scheme seems to us beyond doubt. However there are difficulties to be ironed out in connection with the project and its implementation. There have been many representations and, throughout the years, the exchange of many documents between the government of Saskatchewan and the government of Canada, culminating finally in the month of May last with a clear indication by the last government that no decision had been arrived at. We want to state immediately, with no desire other than the assurance of the protection of the public interest, the proper financing as between this government and the government of Saskatchewan, and the allocation to the province of Saskatchewan and its government of the primary responsibilities for those things which are a provincial responsibility alone, that we intend to proceed at the earliest possible date to the commencement of this project, after it has received-I hope it will-the approval of parliament.
Throughout the years this party has taken a strong and definite stand in this regard. This is one of those things which we are including in our general development plan for expansion in our country and the equalization of opportunity. This is a project which deserves primary consideration.
We start with the maritimes and there is the province of Saskatchewan project to which I have just referred, and then there will of course be considered the great Columbia river plan in the province of British Columbia, respecting which further will be said at a later date. Today we are endeavouring to bring about a favourable settlement of the international problems that are incident to an international river in order to clear the way for a joint program so that the province of British Columbia may be able to develop this power project for the benefit, not only of the people of British Columbia but of the people of Canada as a whole.
These are but few of the major matters which will be dealt with during this session. As far as the international situation is concerned I intended to say no more at this time. Having regard to the developments that are now taking place and which have taken place in recent weeks we must not become apathetic. The international field still holds its grasp on the hearts of all mankind.
My hope is that while the disarmament program offered by the nations of the free world was turned down by the U.S.S.R., in the United Nations today there is springing

up a feeling that serious reconsideration must be given, and will be given, to the whole question of disarmament. We must not allow ourselves to become frightened as a result of this moon that passes by us several times a day, but we must, each and every one of us, so dedicate ourselves to our cause that it cannot be said of us that we did not make our maximum contribution and go to the extreme limits in securing agreement consistent with our security and the maintenance of freedom.
We of Canada, realizing that we live in the tremendous peril of a surprise attack, as do our neighbours in the United States, laid before the disarmament committee-as I also did before the United Nations-Canada's willingness to render open for inspection all parts of the Arctic, providing some correlated action was taken by the U.S.S.R. That would have been a step forward and would have provided for the initiation of a more widely accepted disarmament plan. The suggestion that was advanced by those five countries composing the committee was turned down. We in Canada believe that we went to the very limit in that direction in order to make it apparent to the world and to the U.S.S.R. that we at least, having regard to our strategic position-and we were joined in this by the United States equally-have nothing to hide and that our joint purposes with the United States on this continent are peaceful and not aggressive.
I am looking forward to an opportunity for an early debate on international affairs wherein, providing the electors elect him to the House of Commons, Dr. Sidney Smith will be able to present to parliament as he is now presenting to the United Nations the policies of this country in regard to external affairs.
The Leader of the Opposition said today that in general there is no disagreement regarding external affairs. That has always been our stand. We have endeavoured to the limit of our responsibilities while in opposition so to chart our course that in the international field the nations would know that when the hon. member for Algoma East and those associated with him spoke in the United Nations they were speaking for Canada, and we have not gone back, as was so direfully predicted, in the field of international affairs. Indeed this is indicated by the fact that Canada has in the last few days been chosen a member of the security council, a new responsibility in keeping with Canada's international position.
I intend to conclude by one personal reference. Throughout the years in which I have been in public life, my course has not been directed to personalities or to building up animosities against those on the other side

Leader of the Opposition, by reason of those things that come to us in life, should have found it necessary to take the course that he has.

That is the kind of parliament that the Canadian people ask for; that is the kind of parliament that I hope the Canadian people will receive.

Of course this house today is meeting under extremely interesting circumstances. Apart altogether from the visit of Her Majesty the Queen which we have so much enjoyed, this house is different to any in which I have sat. I have been here since 1935 and this of course is the first time since I have been in this house when no party had a majority. Not since December, 1925 has a party failed to secure a majority of seats in this house.
In January 1926 the government met under somewhat similar but not analagous circumstances. At that time a small group in the house headed by the gentleman who preceded me as leader of the C.C.F., Mr. J. S. Woods-worth, held the balance of power. No party in this house can be said to hold a balance of power in that sense. I recollect that that was a very fruitful parliament. It lasted only six months but during that time our senior citizens received the first indication that this house would grant old age pension legislation and Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, then of Winnipeg North Centre, received that pledge in a letter of which we are rather proud and which we have framed in our national office.
I remember, too, it was in that session that we got the Hudson Bay railway which we in western Canada had looked forward to for many years. We also received a promise of consideration of unemployment insurance. Although it did not come into existence for 14 years we did receive the promise of consideration of it before the house dissolved in July 1926.
As I say, no party in this house today has a position analagous to that then held by Mr. Woodsworth and his friends. We were pleased to find in the speech from the throne reference to increased pensions for our senior citizens with a reduction in the period for qualification. May I add one other thing? Our citizens are paying a fairly substantial premium if it is considered over the working period of life of a young man or woman today. The disqualification on account of residence outside the borders of Canada should, we think, be eliminated as well as the time for qualification reduced as is foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. It is our contention that this pension should be paid as of right.
I regret that in the realm of social security there is no mention of improvement in the national hospitalization plan in the speech from the throne. I look forward to the time when we shall have a comprehensive health plan in this country which will benefit every citizen of this country, regardless of the length of the purse, and provide the best care and treatment that medical science can make available. While we made a short step in the last parliament I should have liked to see the plan extended even if only to the extent of bringing under the hospitalization plan now on the statute books tubercular patients and patients suffering from mental disease.
I could go into other social security measures which I have in mind but I want to speak of some other matters so I must not dwell at too great length on this question. Because of the restrictions of time I am not even going to spend a great deal of time discussing the South Saskatchewan river dam project. I will only say when I was a new member of the house years ago I advocated from my seat on this side of the chamber consideration of irrigation and of a South Saskatchewan river plan. Consequently we are fully in favour of the negotiations for a firm and fair agreement with the government of Saskatchewan and the commencement of the dam at the very earliest possible date.
We are told we have to diversify agriculture and some farmers must get out of wheat production. I may have something more to
say on that subject in a moment but I wish now to comment that irrigation is one way perhaps of taking areas of land out of wheat production and putting them into some other forms of agricultural production.
We in this group also welcome the outlined suggestions in the speech from the throne regarding agriculture. We agree that agricultural returns have been quite inadequate. We agree that our farmers need a proper share of the national income. We even go further than that and say the farmers' share of the national income should be based on a parity price system so that they may receive for their production returns comparable to what they have to pay to produce their crops and to live in our midst. We have been advocating this for a long time in the house and it is again encouraging to know the government intends to go some distance toward the stabilization of agricultural prices even if they do not go the whole distance we would go, in the establishment of a parity price system. I may add that this step forward will receive our support.
Of course we have long advocated advance payments on farm-stored grain. I am under no illusions; we are under no illusions; we know that this is purely a temporary step. It can only mitigate. The advance payments will help the farmer at the beginning of the new crop year, but it is not a solution to the agricultural problems, though it will provide a measure of very welcome relief. A solution can only come from increased sales, increased exports and increased returns. These are not in sight in spite of world food shortages. International agencies point out that there are continuous and increasing food shortages. The world problem is not overproduction; it is surely one of underconsumption. There is, as the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations recognizes, all over the world a problem of underconsumption.
To cut back production in wheat and transfer to cattle, hogs and other farm commodities on a large scale, as proposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), struck me as being a counsel of despair. Ultimately it would merely spread the burden of surpluses around and increase the burden of those surpluses elsewhere. We should be proposing and supporting policies to expand consumption on a world-wide scale.
I am now going to interrupt this trend of thought because I want to move an amendment which I have at hand. If the house will permit me, I shall discuss this amendment

Business of the House when we resume this debate tomorrow. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the following words be added to the address:
This house welcomes the measures indicated in the speech from the throne and urges that these measures be placed before parliament with the least possible delay in order that the benefits proposed therein might accrue to the Canadian people at once. We respectfully submit, however, that in the opinion of this house Your Majesty's advisers should give immediate consideration to the advisability of taking steps to deal with, the menace of inflation, rapidly rising unemployment and other serious problems facing this country. We call upon the government to give immediate effect to the social and economic planning necessary to cope with these problems.
You will observe we believe-and I shall develop this a little later-that we need national social and economic planning. That means, of course, that there must be some public control over our economy and some public direction given to it. I know that hon. gentlemen in various parts of the house have on occasion disagreed with this concept of national planning, but without national planning I am convinced that on a long-term basis the problems that are facing us today can neither be dealt with adequately nor can they be solved.
I would like you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
On motion of Mr. Coldwell the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we intend to ask for interim supply, the need having been explained yesterday by the Minister of Finance. Then, if and when that is agreed to, we shall continue with the debate on the throne speech. In order that we do not lose the time from eleven o'clock to one o'clock, it is necessary that a motion be put

through this afternoon. I would ask unanimous consent to revert to motions in order that I may move a motion to bring about that result.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman unanimous consent to revert to motions?
Agreed.

I move, seconded by the Minister of Finance:
That on Thursday next, government orders shall have precedence over all other business except the ordinary daily routine of business: the house shall meet at 11.00 a.m., and the provisions of standing order 2(1) with respect to the time of meeting shall be suspended in relation thereto.
If that motion were not moved we could not meet until 2.30 p.m. There will be time taken up in considering interim supply and I would hope that later on in the throne speech debate it would be possible to make some arrangement so that we do not lose the whole of tomorrow's time on the throne speech. In other words, if it takes us two hours on interim supply, then we would give that extra time at the conclusion of the regular 10 days.
